claims.question: q1
claims.claim: The team’s repository reached about one million lines and roughly 1,500 merged pull requests in five months with three engineers, averaging 3.5 PRs per engineer per day; throughput increased after the team grew to seven.
claims.quote: Five months later, the repository contains on the order of a million lines of code across application logic, infrastructure, tooling, documentation, and internal developer utilities. Over that period, roughly 1,500 pull requests have been opened and merged with a small team of just three engineers driving Codex. This translates to an average throughput of 3.5 PRs per engineer per day, and surprisingly the throughput has _increased_ as the team has grown to now seven engineers.

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: The team estimates it built the product in about one-tenth the time hand-writing the code would have taken.
claims.quote: We estimate that we built this in about 1/10th the time it would have taken to write the code by hand.

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: As code throughput increased, the team’s bottleneck shifted to human QA capacity.
claims.quote: As code throughput increased, our bottleneck became human QA capacity.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: Instead of a monolithic AGENTS.md encyclopedia, a roughly 100-line AGENTS.md is injected as a table-of-contents map, while a structured docs/ directory is the system of record.
claims.quote:
So instead of treating `AGENTS.md` as the encyclopedia, we treat it as **the table of contents**.

The repository’s knowledge base lives in a structured `docs/` directory treated as the system of record. A short `AGENTS.md` (roughly 100 lines) is injected into context and serves primarily as a map, with pointers to deeper sources of truth elsewhere.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: The team enforces the knowledge base with linters and CI checks, plus a recurring doc-gardening agent that opens fix-up PRs for stale documentation.
claims.quote: We enforce this mechanically. Dedicated linters and CI jobs validate that the knowledge base is up to date, cross-linked, and structured correctly. A recurring “doc-gardening” agent scans for stale or obsolete documentation that does not reflect the real code behavior and opens fix-up pull requests.

claims.question: q3
claims.claim: Human PR review is optional, and almost all review effort has been shifted to agent-to-agent review.
claims.quote: Humans may review pull requests, but aren’t required to. Over time, we’ve pushed almost all review effort towards being handled agent-to-agent.

claims.question: q4
claims.claim: Humans remain in the loop at a different abstraction layer: prioritizing work, translating user feedback into acceptance criteria, and validating outcomes.
claims.quote: Humans always remain in the loop, but work at a different layer of abstraction than we used to. We prioritize work, translate user feedback into acceptance criteria, and validate outcomes.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: Agent autonomy produced drift and “AI slop”; the team initially spent every Friday, 20% of the week, cleaning it up, then encoded golden principles and a recurring cleanup process.
claims.quote:
Initially, humans addressed this manually. Our team used to spend every Friday (20% of the week) cleaning up “AI slop.” Unsurprisingly, that didn’t scale.

Instead, we started encoding what we call “golden principles” directly into the repository and built a recurring cleanup process.
